newsitem.title: USA: U.S. HRW wheat seen withstanding coming cold.
newsitem.headline: U.S. HRW wheat seen withstanding coming cold.

text.p: Most hard red winter wheat in the central U.S. Plains will likely withstand the bitter cold temperatures expected to hit the area later this week, agronomists said Tuesday.
But some crop experts cautioned that winterkill could occur in some of the less hearty varieties of wheat in Kansas and Nebraska, or in fields with low soil moisture levels.
"I don't think this is going to hurt the crop too much," said Cory Falke, fieldman with Collingwood Grain in Sublette, Kan.

"Right now, the wheat's in pretty good shape and it has a lot of secondary roots established," Falke said. "So it's going to have to get awfully cold to really hurt the wheat -- below zero (Farenheit) for several hours, even a day or so."

Tim Bowden, meteorologist at Weather Express in Omaha, Neb., said an Arctic front was due to drop south out of Canada, chilling the northern U.S. Plains Thursday and moving into the central Plains by Friday.
"We're looking at lows Friday night and Saturday morning getting down to zero (degrees Fahrenheit) as far south as the Oklahoma Panhandle," Bowden said.
Bowden said high temperatures Saturday would probably range from five to 10 degrees F in Nebraska to 12 to 18 degrees F in Oklahoma.

Curtis Thompson, crops and soils specialist at the Kansas State University (KSU) extension office in Garden City, Kan., said he would not rule out the possibility of winterkill damage because air temperatures in some areas may be as low as 10 degrees below zero F.
Thompson said wheat plants could be subject to winterkill if the soil temperature around the crown drops into the single digits (F) for an extended period of time.

Plants damaged by winterkill are slow to develop or fail to green up in the spring. Winterkill can occur when air temperatures are cold enough to permeate the soil and damage the crown, the area just below the soil surface where the wheat plant connects to its root system.
Winterkill can also result from heaving, a phenomenon in which successive freezes and thaws disrupt the soil and thereby expose the wheat crown.
Thompson said the risk to the crop this weekend will likely be compounded by the fact that most areas of the central Plains are expected to have little snow cover.
Snow normally serves as a layer of insulation against extreme cold weather.
Thompson said that plants in firm, moist soil were the least at risk, while those in "dry, fluffy soil" were the most vulnerable to winterkill damage.
Randy Brown, crops and soils specialist at the KSU extension office in Colby, Kan., said the wheat in northwest Kansas had gotten off to a strong start and was not likely to suffer from winterkill.
"Unless we have an extremely cold spell, in which we drop below zero for several days, it shouldn't hurt the crop," Brown said.
